IQR|IQR(x)|whisker|outlier|fence: The **interquartile range**: $IQR = Q_3 - Q_1$, the width of the middle 50% of the data (in R, `IQR(x)`). It builds the **fences** that flag **outliers**: lower fence $= Q_1 - 1.5\times IQR$, upper fence $= Q_3 + 1.5\times IQR$. A boxplot's **whisker** extends only to the most extreme data value still inside the fences; anything beyond is drawn as an outlier point. See [IQR, boxplots & outliers](#/math3042/iqr-boxplot-outliers).
Sk|skewed left|skewed right: **Pearson's skewness coefficient**: $Sk = \dfrac{3(\bar{X}-Q_2)}{s}$ (sample) or $\dfrac{3(\mu-Q_2)}{\sigma}$ (population). $Sk = 0$ is symmetric, $Sk < 0$ is **skewed left** (longer tail toward small values, mean below median), $Sk > 0$ is **skewed right** (longer tail toward large values, mean above median); $|Sk| > 1$ is considered highly skewed. See [Skewness](#/math3042/skewness).
Z|unusual: A **Z-score**: $Z = \dfrac{X-\mu}{\sigma}$ (or $\dfrac{X-\bar{X}}{s}$ for sample data) — how many standard deviations $X$ is from the mean. $|Z| > 2$ is flagged **unusual** (outside the $\mu \pm 2\sigma$ band that holds about 95% of normal data), and $|Z| > 3$ is a likely outlier. See [Z-scores & unusual values](#/math3042/z-scores).
P_k|P_{k}|quartile|percentile|five-numbe: The **$k$th percentile**: the value with about $k\%$ of the sorted data at or below it. **Quartiles** are the 25th/50th/75th percentiles ($Q_1, Q_2, Q_3$); the **five-number summary** {minimum, $Q_1$, $Q_2$, $Q_3$, maximum} is what a boxplot draws. See [Quartiles & percentiles](#/math3042/quartiles-percentiles).
coefficient of variation|CV: A unit-free measure of relative spread: $CV = \dfrac{s}{\bar{X}} \times 100\%$ (sample) or $\dfrac{\sigma}{\mu}\times 100\%$ (population). Lets you compare variability between two data sets measured in different units or with different means. See [Coefficient of variation](#/math3042/cv).
normal distribution|empirical rule|\\mu: The **normal distribution** is the symmetric bell-shaped distribution defined by $\mu$ and $\sigma$. The **empirical rule**: for approximately normal data, about 68% falls within $\mu \pm 1\sigma$, about 95% within $\mu \pm 2\sigma$, and about 99.7% within $\mu \pm 3\sigma$. See [68–95–99.7 rule](#/math3042/empirical-rule).
Chebyshev|Chebyshev's rule|1 - \\frac{1}: A distribution-free bound that works for *any* data set, normal or not: at least $1 - \dfrac{1}{k^2}$ of the data lies within $\mu \pm k\sigma$ (e.g. $k=2$ guarantees at least 75%, versus the empirical rule's ~95% for normal data specifically). See [Chebyshev's rule](#/math3042/chebyshev).
quantile()|quantile(x): R function returning percentiles/quartiles of a numeric vector; `quantile(x)` gives the default five-number-summary quartiles, `quantile(x, k/100)` gives the $k$th percentile. See [R from Lab 1](#/math3042/r-essentials).
subset()|subset(df, condition): R function filtering a data frame's rows by a logical condition, e.g. `subset(df, condition)` — the base-R equivalent of `dplyr::filter()`. See [R from Lab 1](#/math3042/r-essentials).
filter()|dplyr::filter(): The `dplyr` package's row-filtering function, e.g. `dplyr::filter(df, condition)`; does the same job as base R's `subset()`. See [R from Lab 1](#/math3042/r-essentials).
histogram|hist(): The most common and important chart for numerical data: the range of $X$ is divided into classes of equal width, the values in each class are counted, and one rectangle per class is drawn with height equal to the frequency, no gaps. R: `hist(x, breaks=seq(lo, hi, by=w), right=FALSE)`. See [Histograms: the class recipe](#/math3042-u2/histograms).
class mark|midpoint: The midpoint of a class, $(\text{lower} + \text{upper})/2$, used as the representative value $X_i$ of every observation in the class when a grouped mean or sd is computed (Unit 1). See [Histograms: the class recipe](#/math3042-u2/histograms).
model formula|~|Days~Sex|~Days: R's `~` notation for "explained by / grouped by": `~Days` means just the Days variable, `Days ~ Sex` means Days grouped by Sex, `Days ~ Eth + Sex` groups by both (names A.F, N.F, A.M, N.M), and `mpg ~ wt` in a plot means Y against X. See [favstats, model formulas, percentiles, Z-scores](#/math3042-u2/lab2-grouped).
favstats|favstats(): mosaic's summary function: `favstats(~Days, data=quine)` prints min, Q1, median, Q3, max, mean, sd, n, missing, and `favstats(Days ~ Lrn, data=quine)` prints one such row per group (AL mean 15.8, SL mean 17.3). Unlike `summary()` it includes the standard deviation. See [favstats, model formulas, percentiles, Z-scores](#/math3042-u2/lab2-grouped).
mosaic: The R package used in Lab 2 that adds `favstats()` and lets `mean`, `median`, `sd`, `var`, `min`, `max`, `sum`, `IQR`, `quantile`, `histogram` and `bwplot` take a model formula and `data=`, so statistics can be computed per group. See [favstats, model formulas, percentiles, Z-scores](#/math3042-u2/lab2-grouped).
bwplot|bwplot(): lattice/mosaic box-and-whisker plot: `bwplot(~Days, data=quine, horizontal=TRUE)` for one box, `bwplot(Days ~ Eth, data=quine)` for side-by-side boxes per group. The dot marks the median and circles beyond the whiskers are outliers. See [favstats, model formulas, percentiles, Z-scores](#/math3042-u2/lab2-grouped).
prop.table|prop.table(): Turns a table of counts into fractions of the total: `prop.table(table(P25.students$Sex))` gives F 0.622, M 0.378 among the quarter of students with the fewest absences. See [favstats, model formulas, percentiles, Z-scores](#/math3042-u2/lab2-grouped).
complement|complement rule: $\bar{A} = S - A$ is everything in $S$ not in $A$, and $P(\bar{A}) = 1 - P(A)$. Use it for 'at least one' and 'less than the maximum'. See [The complement and addition rules](#/math3042-u3/complement-addition).
addition rule: $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$: the overlap is subtracted so it is not counted twice. For mutually exclusive events it is $P(A) + P(B)$. See [The complement and addition rules](#/math3042-u3/complement-addition).
mutually exclusive: Two events that cannot both occur in one trial (a black card and a heart): $P(A \cap B) = 0$. Mutually exclusive events with positive probabilities are always dependent. See [The complement and addition rules](#/math3042-u3/complement-addition).
conditional probability: $P(B \mid A) = |A \cap B| / |A| = P(A \cap B)/P(A)$: the probability of $B$ when the sample space is restricted to $A$. On a two-way table, a cell over its row or column total. See [Conditional probability, independence, the multiplication rule](#/math3042-u3/conditional-independence).
independent|independence: Events with $P(A \cap B) = P(A)\,P(B)$, equivalently $P(B \mid A) = P(B)$: knowing $A$ does not change the probability of $B$. Right-handed and iPhone in the notes are dependent ($0.732 \ne 0.702$). See [Conditional probability, independence, the multiplication rule](#/math3042-u3/conditional-independence).
multiplication rule: $P(A \cap B) = P(A)\,P(B \mid A)$ in general, $P(A)\,P(B)$ when independent: two Aces are $1/169$ with replacement and $1/221$ without. See [Conditional probability, independence, the multiplication rule](#/math3042-u3/conditional-independence).
law of total probability|total probabili: $P(B) = \sum_i P(A_i)\,P(B \mid A_i)$: add every path of the tree that ends in $B$; $P(\text{defective}) = 0.0085 + 0.0030 + 0.0010 = 0.0125$. See [Bayes' rule on a tree diagram](#/math3042-u3/bayes).
Bayes' rule|Bayes' theorem|Bayes: $P(A_i \mid B) = P(A_i)\,P(B \mid A_i) / \sum_j P(A_j)\,P(B \mid A_j)$: reverses a conditional probability by dividing one path of the tree by the total probability of $B$; $P(\text{Intel} \mid \text{defective}) = 0.0085/0.0125 = 0.68$. See [Bayes' rule on a tree diagram](#/math3042-u3/bayes).
without replacement: Each draw removes an item, so later probabilities change: two Aces are $(4/52)(3/51)$, and `sample(deck, n)` without `replace=TRUE`. See [Conditional probability, independence, the multiplication rule](#/math3042-u3/conditional-independence).
sample|sample()|sample.int: `sample(x, n, replace=TRUE, prob=)` draws $n$ values from `x`; `sample.int(6, n, replace=TRUE)` rolls $n$ dice. `replace=TRUE` allows repeats (dice, coins); omit it for cards; `prob=` loads the die. See [Lab 4: simulating probabilities](#/math3042-u3/lab4-simulations).
replicate|replicate(): `replicate(m, expr)` evaluates `expr` $m$ times and returns the results as a vector, replacing a for loop whose body ignores its index. See [Lab 4: simulating probabilities](#/math3042-u3/lab4-simulations).
function|function(): `name <- function(args) { ...; return(value) }` defines an R function such as `Prob.Heads(m)` or `Roll.Some.Dice(m, n)`. See [Lab 4: simulating probabilities](#/math3042-u3/lab4-simulations).
discrete probability distribution|probab: tells us $P(x)$ for any possible value $x$; given by a table/histogram or a formula; requires $\sum P(x) = 1$ and $0 \le P(x) \le 1$. See [Discrete random variables, their distributions, mean and standard deviation](#/math3042-u4/discrete-distributions).
expected value|E[X]|mean of a random var: $\mu = \sum_x x \cdot P(x)$, the mean of $X$ over all possible outcomes weighted by probability; a sample mean of simulated values approaches it. See [Discrete random variables, their distributions, mean and standard deviation](#/math3042-u4/discrete-distributions).
variance of a random variable|standard d: $\sigma^2 = \sum_x (x - \mu)^2 P(x)$ and $\sigma = \sqrt{\sigma^2}$. See [Discrete random variables, their distributions, mean and standard deviation](#/math3042-u4/discrete-distributions).
binomial distribution: the distribution of $X$ = the number of successes in $n$ independent trials with the same $p$: $P(x) = nCx \cdot p^x q^{n-x}$, $\mu = np$, $\sigma^2 = npq$. See [Binomial experiments and the binomial formula](#/math3042-u4/binomial).
hypergeometric distribution: $X$ = number of successes in $n$ draws *without replacement* from a finite population of $N$ with $K$ successes: $P(x) = C(K,x)\,C(N-K,\,n-x)/C(N,n)$, $\mu = nK/N$, $\sigma^2 = n \frac{K}{N} \frac{N-K}{N} \frac{N-n}{N-1}$. See [Hypergeometric: sampling without replacement, and the 5% rule](#/math3042-u4/hypergeometric).
5% rule: if the sample size $n$ is 5 % or less of the population $N$, hypergeometric and binomial probabilities are practically the same. See [Hypergeometric: sampling without replacement, and the 5% rule](#/math3042-u4/hypergeometric).
geometric distribution: $X$ = the number of trials it takes to obtain the first success: $P(X = x) = q^{x-1} p$ for $x = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$; $\mu = 1/p$, $\sigma^2 = (1-p)/p^2$. See [Geometric: trials until the first success](#/math3042-u4/geometric).
Poisson distribution: the number of occurrences of an event over an interval when occurrences are uniform, independent and the mean $\lambda$ is known: $P(X = x) = \frac{\lambda^x}{x!} e^{-\lambda}$, $\mu = \lambda$, $\sigma^2 = \lambda$. See [Poisson: counts per interval](#/math3042-u4/poisson).
dbinom|pbinom: R's binomial probability `dbinom(x, n, p)` and cumulative `pbinom(x, n, p)` $= P(X \le x)$; `dhyper(x, K, N-K, n)`, `dgeom(x-1, p)` (R counts failures, so subtract 1), `dpois(x, lambda)` follow the same d/p pattern. See [Which distribution, and the R function for each](#/math3042-u4/choosing-distribution).
rbinom|rbinom(): `rbinom(m, n, p)` draws $m$ random binomial counts, each the number of successes in $n$ trials with success probability $p$; `rbinom(1, n, p)/n` is one simulated sample proportion. See [R on paper](#/math3042-midterm/r-on-paper).
rhyper|rhyper(): `rhyper(m, K, N-K, n)` draws $m$ random hypergeometric counts: successes in a sample of $n$ taken without replacement from a population with $K$ successes and $N-K$ failures. See [R on paper](#/math3042-midterm/r-on-paper).
rpois|rpois(): `rpois(m, lambda)` draws $m$ random Poisson counts with mean $\lambda$ for the interval. See [R on paper](#/math3042-midterm/r-on-paper).
rgeom|rgeom(): `rgeom(m, p)` draws $m$ random counts of failures before the first success; add 1 (`rgeom(m, p) + 1`) for the course's trial number. See [R on paper](#/math3042-midterm/r-on-paper).
lower.tail|lower.tail = FALSE|lower.tail: an argument of every `p` function; `lower.tail = FALSE` returns $P(X > k)$ instead of $P(X \le k)$, so `phyper(11, 42, 270, 20, lower.tail = FALSE)` equals `1 - phyper(11, 42, 270, 20)`. See [R on paper](#/math3042-midterm/r-on-paper).
expected profit|net payoff|expected winn: the expected value of the net outcome per play, $\mu = \sum x\,P(x)$ with $x$ = prize minus cost (or payout minus premium); a negative value is an expected loss per play. See [Expected value in dollars, the variance shortcut, Poisson across separate intervals](#/math3042-midterm/expected-dollars-shortcuts).
variance shortcut|shortcut formula: $\sigma^2 = \sum x^2 P(x) - \mu^2$, printed on the formula sheet; gives the same value as $\sum (x-\mu)^2 P(x)$ when $\mu$ is carried unrounded. See [Expected value in dollars, the variance shortcut, Poisson across separate intervals](#/math3042-midterm/expected-dollars-shortcuts).
